metaTitle: Camel Spider (Sun Spider): Size, Bite and Myths
metaDescription: Camel spiders are fast desert arachnids, not true spiders. Their real size and speed, the bite, where they live in the US, and each myth checked.
h1: Camel Spiders (Sun Spiders): What They Are, How Big They Get, Bites and Myths
dek: Camel spiders, also called sun spiders and wind scorpions, are desert arachnids with huge jaws and no venom glands. Their real size and speed, the bite, where they live in the US, the look-alikes, and each myth checked.
excerpt: What camel spiders are, how big and fast they really get, what a bite does, where they live in the US, and how to tell them from wolf spiders, tarantulas and scorpions.

quickAnswer.lead: **A camel spider is not a true spider but a fast desert arachnid with huge jaws pointing forward and two leg-like palps that make it look ten-legged; it spins no silk and has no stinger and no venom glands.** It can give a painful bite if handled, says the [Defense Centers for Public Health–Aberdeen (DCPH-A)](https://ph.health.mil/topics/entomology/what/Pages/Camel-Spider.aspx).
bullets: Camel spiders in the western US are 5/8 to 1 3/4 inches long (15 to 45 mm) and light tan to brown, says [University of Arizona Cooperative Extension](https://www.extension.arizona.edu/sites/extension.arizona.edu/files/attachment/Sopulgids.pdf); DCPH-A says the largest species anywhere reach no more than 6 inches with legs outstretched.

In the US they live mainly in dry country: [UC IPM](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/windscorpion/) says they are common in California's San Joaquin Valley and the arid Southwest, and [Colorado State University Extension](https://extension.colostate.edu/topic-areas/insects/sunspiders-windscorpions-5-589/) counts 15 species in Colorado.

UC IPM says they are active mostly at night, and DCPH-A says they run toward lights, flashlights and campfires included; Colorado State says outdoor lighting near a foundation may often contribute to finding one indoors.

The scary stories are myths: they do not scream, run 25 mph or eat camels, according to [the Burke Museum](https://www.burkemuseum.org/collections-and-research/biology/arachnology-and-entomology/spider-myths/myth-too-many-camel-spider) and DCPH-A.
To remove one, UC IPM says to trap it under a jar, slide paper underneath and release it outdoors; it recommends no chemical control.

body.text: What is a camel spider?

A camel spider is an arachnid but not a true spider: it belongs to an order of its own, Solifugae, and also goes by sun spider, wind scorpion, solpugid and solifugid. [The Defense Centers for Public Health–Aberdeen (DCPH-A)](https://ph.health.mil/topics/entomology/what/Pages/Camel-Spider.aspx), part of the US Department of Defense, says solifugids are not spiders, scorpions or insects, and counts over 1,000 species, most of them in hot deserts.

body.alt: Camel spider on a white background: an orange-tan head with huge jaws pointing forward, long leg-like palps, pale spiny legs and a plump, segmented gray-brown abdomen
body.caption: A solifuge, or camel spider, found under a rock by day in Trinidad, Colorado, and shown on white; its finder put it at very roughly 1 inch long, jaws included. Look for the forward jaws and the leg-like palps.

body.text: [UC IPM's Pest Notes on the windscorpion](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/windscorpion/) says it has no venom glands or web-spinning organs, so it never builds a web, and, unlike a scorpion, no stinger or pincers. Silk-spinning organs and a distinct abdomen are what set spiders apart from the other arachnids, [Texas A&M AgriLife Extension's spider guide](https://agrilifeextension.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Spiders-1.pdf) explains, and [the guide to arachnids and insects](/blog/are-ticks-arachnids-or-insects) shows where ticks and scorpions fit.

In the US they are mainly animals of the dry West and Southwest. [University of Arizona Cooperative Extension](https://www.extension.arizona.edu/sites/extension.arizona.edu/files/attachment/Sopulgids.pdf) calls solpugids beneficial predators related to spiders, with more than 120 species described in North America and over 50 in the southwestern US.
How do you identify a camel spider?

Look at the front end. A camel spider has huge jaws sticking straight out from its head and, in front of its legs, a pair of long, leg-like palps (pedipalps), so it seems to have ten legs. [Colorado State University Extension's sunspider fact sheet](https://extension.colostate.edu/topic-areas/insects/sunspiders-windscorpions-5-589/) says the pedipalps look like a fifth pair of legs.

body.title: Is it a camel spider? Five checks
items: **Jaws.** Large, pincer-like jaws (chelicerae) that point forward and work up and down like pliers (UC IPM; University of Arizona).
**Ten legs, or so it seems.** Eight legs plus two leg-like palps; UC IPM says it walks on the last three pairs and uses the first pair as feelers.
**Two eyes.** The University of Arizona describes two distinct eyes; Texas A&M says most spiders have eight.
**Body.** A head section and a plump, 10-segmented abdomen, light tan to brown, often with a darker abdomen (University of Arizona; DCPH-A).
**No web, no stinger.** It spins no silk and has no stinger (UC IPM); a tail with a stinger means a scorpion.

body.text: Behavior helps too. UC IPM says windscorpions run swiftly and are active mostly at night, and the University of Arizona says they run carrying the palps above the body. DCPH-A says the sticky palp tips help them catch prey and climb smooth surfaces such as glass.

body.text: How big and how fast are camel spiders really?

Most US camel spiders are under 2 inches long. The University of Arizona gives 5/8 to 1 3/4 inches (15 to 45 mm) for the western US, UC IPM gives 3/4 to 1 1/2 inches for California, and Colorado State gives about 1 1/2 inches with legs extended for Colorado. A big one: a male *Eremocosta striata* from Pima County, Arizona, documented by [Texas A&M AgriLife Extension's El Paso County office](https://elp.tamu.edu/ipm/bugs/windscorpions/05-class-arachnida-solifugae-eremobatidae-eremocosta-striata-windscorpions-male-tarsus-of-fourth-pair-of-legs/), measured about 1 3/4 inches (43 mm) with its jaws and about 3 2/3 inches (93 mm) across the legs.

body.alt: Large tan camel spider with big jaws resting on an open palm
body.caption: A camel spider, *Eremocosta striata*, on an open hand at an insect event in Pima County, Arizona, which shows its size and its big jaws. Don't try this at home: DCPH-A says not to pick one up.
body.credit: (c) Wendy McCrady, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: The biggest species anywhere are not giants either: DCPH-A says the largest is no more than 6 inches (15 cm) long with legs outstretched, and [the Burke Museum's camel spider myth page](https://www.burkemuseum.org/collections-and-research/biology/arachnology-and-entomology/spider-myths/myth-too-many-camel-spider), by Rod Crawford, puts the maximum body length of Near Eastern solpugids at about 2 inches (5 cm).

The famous giants were a camera trick. A photo of two camel spiders mass-emailed in April 2004, said to come from someone stationed in Baghdad, showed animals around 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) long, according to a correspondent the Burke Museum cites, made to look 8 to 10 times life size by false perspective.

Speed is the other exaggeration. The Burke Museum says the highest speed cited in scientific sources is 10 mph and that the only accurately measured speeds Crawford found were under 1 mph; DCPH-A says about a mile an hour, not the 25 mph of the email stories. Still, Colorado State says they can run down most prey, and the University of Arizona says their speed makes them hard to trap.
Which camel spider myths are false?

Nearly all of the frightening ones. Many spread by email during the Iraq war, and the Burke Museum traces the numbing-venom story to an earlier Gulf War myth. Here is each claim against what the Burke Museum and DCPH-A say.

head: The claim
What the sources say
rows: As big as dinner plates
False. The largest species is no more than 6 inches long with legs outstretched (DCPH-A).
They run 25 mph
False. 10 mph is the top figure in scientific sources, and the only accurately measured speeds found were under 1 mph (Burke Museum).
They jump 6 feet high
False. Their jumping is poor (DCPH-A) and nothing special (Burke Museum).
They scream as they run
False. They cannot scream (DCPH-A); some species make a barely audible buzz or hiss (Burke Museum).
They chase people
No. They head for shade, including a moving human shadow (DCPH-A; Burke Museum).
They eat camels' stomachs
False. They do not feed on large animals such as camels or people, and they lay their eggs in soil (Burke Museum).
Their venom numbs you and rots flesh
False. They have no venom glands (DCPH-A; UC IPM); a bite that breaks the skin can become infected (Burke Museum).
body.caption: Each answer comes from the sources named in its row, linked in the text of this page.

body.text: The chasing story has a simple explanation: DCPH-A says solifugids follow a moving human shadow, so they seem to give chase, and the Burke Museum says one running toward a person in the hot desert sun is looking for shade.
Do camel spiders bite, and can the bite break the skin?

They can bite, but they have no venom. UC IPM says a windscorpion bites only in self-defense, when handled or restrained, and can't seriously harm people. DCPH-A says solifugids have no venom glands but can give a painful bite if cornered or handled.

Whether a bite breaks the skin is where the sources differ, and size may explain it. Colorado State, describing Colorado's windscorpions, which reach about 1 1/2 inches with legs extended, says a bite is rare and no more than a mild pinch that cannot break the skin. DCPH-A says the larger species can easily puncture and tear skin and that secondary infections may follow, and the Burke Museum says a bite that does break the skin is likely to become infected, which disinfectant can prevent.

So treat a bite that breaks the skin as a wound. For insect and spider bites, [Poison Control](https://www.poison.org/articles/insect-and-spider-bites) advises washing with soap and water, putting cold water or a cloth filled with ice on it for 10 to 20 minutes, and watching for pus, swollen glands, and swelling, redness or pain that gets worse.

body.title: When to get help for a bite
body.text: Poison Control says to seek help if symptoms at the bite worsen significantly, if you have symptoms beyond the bite, or if you have a history of allergic reactions. In the US, call 1-800-222-1222 or use its online tool. If a bite looks infected, see a healthcare provider.

For the spiders whose bites do matter in the US, see [the guide to venomous spiders](/blog/venomous-spiders); for photos of spider bites, see [what a spider bite looks like](/blog/what-does-a-spider-bite-look-like).
Where do camel spiders live in the US?

Mainly in the dry West and Southwest. UC IPM says windscorpions are common in California's San Joaquin Valley and the arid parts of the Southwest, the University of Arizona counts over 50 species in the southwestern US, and Colorado State says 15 species live in the drier areas of Colorado below 7,500 feet.

By day they hide under rocks, boards, logs, cow chips and plant stalks or in rodent burrows, Colorado State says. UC IPM says they are active mostly at night but may be seen by day, and DCPH-A says some species are active only by day. The guides to [spiders in Arizona](/blog/spiders-in-arizona) and [spiders in California](/blog/spiders-in-california) cover the true spiders there.
What do camel spiders eat?

Small insects and other arthropods, which Colorado State says they find by touch or vibration. The University of Arizona adds spiders and the occasional scorpion or centipede, noting that they have been known to eat each other, and DCPH-A says the diet sometimes includes small lizards. They crush prey with the jaws and, the University of Arizona says, suck out its body fluids.

Because they eat insects, UC IPM and the University of Arizona regard them as beneficial. Colorado State assumes a one-year life cycle for Colorado's windscorpions: a female lays one mass of 50 to 200 eggs in a burrow, typically in late summer, and is thought to die soon after; the young hatch in 1 to 2 weeks and stay in the burrow a couple of weeks before leaving to hunt.
Why is there a camel spider on my porch or in my garage?

Often lights, and the insects drawn to them. Colorado State says outdoor lighting near a foundation may often contribute to windscorpions turning up indoors, as they hunt insects the lights attract, though their getting in is infrequent, mostly in mid to late summer. DCPH-A says they run toward any light at night, and Texas A&M's El Paso County office notes that its Arizona specimen was attracted to mercury vapor and ultraviolet lights.

Indoors, the University of Arizona says, one is either hunting insects such as crickets or looking for a way back out, and some ride in on firewood or other things stored outside. UC IPM says they can turn up on roads and paths and sometimes enter buildings.

body.text: What looks like a camel spider?
Four other ground hunters get mistaken for camel spiders, and a basement insect shares the name. The quick-ID table at the top compares them.
Wolf spider

A true spider with eight eyes: Texas A&M describes a front row of four tiny eyes, a larger pair behind them, often two dark stripes on the head section, and a length of 1/2 to 3 inches. Wolf spiders hunt after dark and commonly slip indoors under doors. See [the wolf spider guide](/blog/wolf-spiders).

body.alt: Face-on close-up of a young wolf spider: two large, shiny black eyes above a row of four small ones, two more eyes set back near the top, and hairy brown fangs below
body.caption: A young wetland giant wolf spider, Tigrosa helluo, face-on in Chester County, Pennsylvania. Count the eyes: two large ones above a row of four small ones, plus two set back near the top.
body.credit: (c) Meghan Cassidy, some rights reserved (CC BY-SA), via iNaturalist

body.text: Tarantula

Bigger and hairy all over. [UC IPM's Pest Notes on spiders](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/spiders/) gives tarantulas a body 1 to 2 inches long and says they wait at a burrow entrance at night, while males wander looking for females. Texas A&M says the Texas brown tarantula's legs can span more than 3 inches and that the bite is not dangerous, though hairs from the abdomen can irritate skin and eyes. See [the tarantula guide](/blog/tarantulas).
Scorpion

Pincers and a stinger. [UC IPM's scorpion Pest Note](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/scorpions/) describes a crablike animal with a pair of pincers, four pairs of legs and a long, segmented tail ending in a stinger; scorpions hunt at night and glow under a black light. The bark scorpion grows to about 3 inches, and UC IPM says anyone stung by one should seek medical attention. See [what to do about a scorpion sting](/blog/scorpion-stings).

body.alt: Slender, pale tan Arizona bark scorpion seen from above on coarse sand, with long, thin pincers and a segmented tail curled at the tip
body.caption: An Arizona bark scorpion, Centruroides sculpturatus, on sand in Picacho, Arizona. Look for the pincers and the long, segmented tail ending in a stinger, which a camel spider never has.

body.text: Whip scorpion (vinegaroon)

No stinger, and a whip for a tail. [UF/IFAS Extension's giant whip scorpion profile](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN890) describes an arachnid of Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Oklahoma and Florida up to 2 inches long, not counting the tail, with large pincer-like palps. It has no venom, sprays concentrated acetic acid from the base of its tail and can give a noticeable pinch if mishandled.

body.needed: A giant whip scorpion (vinegaroon), Mastigoproctus giganteus, on the ground in Arizona, New Mexico or Texas, showing the thick pincer-like palps and the thin, whip-like tail; public domain or CC0

body.text: Camel cricket

It shares only the name. [Clemson Extension](https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/camel-crickets/) describes camel crickets as wingless, humpbacked insects 1/2 to 1 1/2 inches long, with antennae much longer than the body and big jumping hind legs, found indoors in damp basements, crawl spaces and garages. See [the camel cricket guide](/blog/camel-crickets).
Still unsure? [The spider identifier](/tools/spider-identifier) asks seven questions, and the camel spider is among its results.

body.text: What should you do with a camel spider in the house?

Catch it and put it outside; there is no need to spray. UC IPM says to place a jar over it, slip a piece of paper under the jar and release it outdoors, and recommends no chemical control; the University of Arizona also says pesticides are not recommended. Do not try to pick one up, DCPH-A says, and brush one off rather than swatting it.

items: **Seal the way in.** Seal cracks around the foundation and under doors (UC IPM), and check weather stripping and the gaps where utility lines enter (University of Arizona).
**Dim outdoor lights.** Colorado State says less outdoor lighting plus sealed entry points near ground level should keep most out.
**Find their food.** If they keep turning up inside, look for the indoor insects feeding them and check firewood you bring in, the University of Arizona says.
**In camp, shake things out.** DCPH-A advises shaking out shoes, sleeping bags and clothing before use, and never walking barefoot outdoors.

body.text: [Keeping spiders out of the house](/blog/how-to-keep-spiders-out-of-your-house) covers sealing gaps in more detail.

body.title: Catch it for a closer look
body.text: Trap it under a clear jar, slide stiff paper underneath and photograph it beside a ruler marked in inches, checking for the forward-pointing jaws and the leg-like palps. Your county's cooperative extension office can help identify it.

faqs.question: Are camel spiders harmful to humans?
faqs.answer: Not seriously. UC IPM says windscorpions can't seriously harm people, and DCPH-A says that apart from the painful pinch they can give a careless person, solifugids pose no threat to humans at all. They have no venom glands and bite only when handled, cornered or restrained. The one real risk is infection: DCPH-A says larger species can puncture and tear skin and that secondary infections may follow, so clean any bite that breaks the skin and watch it.

faqs.question: Are camel spiders aggressive?
faqs.answer: They can look it, but they do not go after people. Colorado State says windscorpions do not attack and bite only if accidentally restrained, and UC IPM says they bite only in self-defense when handled. DCPH-A calls solifugids very aggressive and able to give a painful bite if cornered or handled, yet also says they are generally harmless to people. One that runs toward a person standing in the desert sun is looking for shade, the Burke Museum says.

faqs.question: Are camel spiders poisonous?
faqs.answer: No, and they are not venomous either. UC IPM and DCPH-A say they have no venom glands, Colorado State says they have no poison glands, and the University of Arizona says none are known to have venom. The Burke Museum calls the story of a numbing venom that makes flesh rot a myth, built on an earlier one from the Gulf War. What they do have is powerful jaws, which crush their prey.

faqs.question: What happens if a camel spider bites you?
faqs.answer: Usually a painful pinch and nothing more, since they have no venom. Colorado State says a bite from one of Colorado's windscorpions cannot break the skin, but DCPH-A says larger species can puncture and tear skin and that secondary infections may follow. For bites, Poison Control advises washing with soap and water, applying cold for 10 to 20 minutes, watching for pus, swollen glands or worsening redness, swelling and pain, and seeking help if symptoms worsen significantly.

faqs.question: Are camel spiders really as big as the pictures?
faqs.answer: No. The giant camel spiders in a photo mass-emailed in April 2004 were around 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) long, according to a correspondent the Burke Museum cites, and only looked 8 to 10 times life size because of false perspective. DCPH-A says the largest species anywhere is no more than 6 inches long with legs outstretched, and the University of Arizona gives 5/8 to 1 3/4 inches for those in the western US.

faqs.question: How fast is a camel spider?
faqs.answer: Fast enough to run down most prey, Colorado State says, but far slower than the stories. Rod Crawford of the Burke Museum says the highest speed cited in scientific sources is 10 mph and that the only accurately measured speeds he could find were under 1 mph, and DCPH-A puts their running speed at about a mile an hour. The 25 mph figure that circulates online is a myth.

faqs.question: Why do camel spiders chase people?
faqs.answer: They are not chasing anyone. DCPH-A says solifugids follow a moving human shadow, which makes it seem as if they are giving chase, and the Burke Museum says one that runs toward a person standing in the hot desert sun is looking for shade to hide in. At night, DCPH-A adds, they run toward any light source, including flashlights and campfires.

faqs.question: Do camel spiders scream?
faqs.answer: No. DCPH-A lists stalking people while screaming among the myths and says solifugids cannot scream; the loudest noise they make is their jaws crunching prey. The Burke Museum says some species can make a barely audible stridulation that sounds like a buzz or hiss, nothing like the screaming described in follow-ups to the 2004 email that spread many of these stories.

faqs.question: Is a camel spider a spider or a scorpion?
faqs.answer: Neither. DCPH-A says solifugids are neither spiders nor scorpions, and not insects either: they are arachnids in an order of their own, Solifugae. UC IPM says that, unlike spiders, a windscorpion has no venom glands or web-spinning organs, and that unlike scorpions it has no pincers or stinger. The University of Arizona describes them as somewhat resembling scorpions without claws or stingers.

faqs.question: Why are they called camel spiders?
faqs.answer: None of the sources here settles where the name came from, but they agree on what it does not mean. The Burke Museum lists the claim that they are named for eating camels' stomachs among the myths and says they do not feed on large animals such as camels, and DCPH-A calls the story that they lay eggs in and eat the bellies of camels fiction. The other common name, windscorpion, comes from their speed, UC IPM says.
